stories.title: Recycling of spent SCR catalysts by near-complete tungsten and vanadium extraction via mechanochemical alkali conversion and water leaching
stories.description: Spent WO3–V2O5/TiO2 selective catalytic reduction (SCR) catalysts are an important secondary source of tungsten (W) and vanadium (V), but under moderate direct alkaline-leaching conditions, V is often extracted more readily than W because supported W-bearing species may remain incompletely converted. In this work, mechanochemical alkali conversion (MCC) followed by water leaching was developed to improve extraction of both metals, particularly W. Spent SCR catalysts were milled with NaOH in a high-energy ball mill and subsequently leached with water at room temperature. A 33 factorial design with ANOVA revealed that NaOH/SCR mass ratio and milling intensity were highly significant for both metals (P < 0.001), whereas milling media size had only a minor effect within the explored range. Linear regression models described the data well (R2 ≈ 0.81 for V and 0.95 for W). Extraction ranged from 86.9 to 100% for V and 39.4–99.6% for W, confirming the stronger sensitivity of W to process severity. Under optimized conditions (NaOH/SCR = 1.6, 1000 rpm, 2 mm media), near-quantitative extraction of both metals (≈ 99–100%) was achieved by water leaching at room temperature. The aqueous step reached a plateau within 5 min, and reducing the liquid-to-solid ratio from 100 to 10 mL/g did not decrease extraction, indicating that overall performance was governed mainly by the prior solid-state conversion. Additional analysis of milling time and cumulative energy input showed that V conversion responded rapidly, whereas W conversion remained more dependent on milling severity and impact intensity.

stories.title: Tracking funding disparities in global health aid with machine learning
stories.description: Reducing the global burden of disease is crucial for improving health outcomes. However, misalignment between health aid and country-level disease burden leaves vulnerable populations without the necessary support for major health challenges, particularly in the least developed countries. Here, we develop a machine learning pipeline using large language models to track flows in official development assistance (ODA) earmarked for health and identify aid–burden misalignment. We classified 3.7 million development aid projects from 2000 to 2022 (USD  ~ 332 billion) into 17 major categories of communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases (CMNNDs) and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). We compared the rank of per capita ODA disbursement against the rank of disease burden, measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). We interpret DALY-based alignment as a policy-relevant heuristic rather than a prescriptive allocation criterion. Although funding and disease burden are significantly correlated for many diseases, there are notable disparities. For example, NCDs account for 59.5% of global DALYs but received only 2.5% of health-related ODA over the study period. This is concerning because low- and middle-income countries face an increasing double burden from both CMNNDs and NCDs. Our results show aid–burden misalignment across multiple diseases in several regions, including Central Africa and parts of South Asia and West Africa. Overall, our results identify health disparities to potentially inform policy decisions on development assistance and support targeted allocation of health aid. Misalignment between health aid and country-level disease burden can leave populations without the necessary support for major health challenges. Here the authors report a machine learning analysis of global health aid and conclude that aid is often misaligned with country-level disease burden, with non-communicable diseases receiving limited aid despite their large global burden.

stories.title: Thermal effects of molten brass exposure on human teeth and noble alloy metal-ceramic restorations: an experimental forensic study
stories.description: Dental and prosthetic structures are well recognized in forensic contexts for their contribution to the identification of human remains. In such scenarios, valuable information may be obtained from metal–ceramic crowns fabricated with noble alloys. Based on judicial cases involving the suspected disappearance of bodies in foundries, the aim of this study was to evaluate the behavior and structural changes of these restorations when exposed to elevated temperatures, with particular emphasis on exposure to molten metals, as may occur in industrial or metallurgical environments. This experimental study evaluated the thermal behavior of metal–ceramic crowns with noble alloys (gold–platinum–palladium) cemented on extracted human teeth. The study was conducted on 200 dental samples extracted for therapeutic reasons and subsequently analyzed under controlled experimental conditions. All extractions were performed exclusively for clinical indications, and all donors provided written informed consent for the scientific use of the extracted teeth, which were fully anonymized prior to experimentation. Samples were subjected to immersion in molten brass at 980 °C for predefined time intervals. Morphological integrity, structural alterations, and prosthesis–tooth interactions were assessed after thermal exposure. Noble alloy metal–ceramic crowns demonstrated high resistance to extreme temperatures, maintaining structural integrity despite surface oxidation and decementation of the prosthetic component.. Dental roots showed variable degrees of preservation, with identifiable morphological features remaining detectable even after prolonged exposure. The tooth–prosthesis complex exhibits significant thermal resistance under extreme thermal exposure conditions comparable to those encountered in metallurgical environments. These preliminary findings suggest that noble alloy metal–ceramic restorations may represent potential forensic markers and may contribute to personal identification under thermal conditions comparable to those investigated in the present study.
